extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide offering definitions and usage guidance for terms relating to race, religion, gender, disability, sexuality and culture, with recommendations on preferred, avoidable or contextual language for reporting. It explains origins, meanings and when to use or avoid specific words and labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: pink triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Now a gay pride symbol, it was the symbol gay men were required to wear in Nazi concentration camps during World War II. Lesbians sometimes also use a black triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides historical origin and contemporary usage as a pride symbol; implies sensitivity to Holocaust history when using the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polock, Polack
rubrics_metrics.description: A derogatory word for a Pole or a person of Polish descent. The word derives from Polak, which means a Polish male or a person of Polish nationality, which has a neutral connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the slur; recognize its origin and neutral alternatives. Example of cultural usage in 'All in the Family' noted as historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: polyamorous
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in more than one consensual intimate relationship at a time, or being non-monogamous. Not to be confused with pansexual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accurately; distinguish from other sexual-orientation/relationship terms like pansexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: polygamy
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of having more than one spouse at a time. It was practiced by Mormons in the 1800s but was officially outlawed by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in 1890. Members who are polygamists are excommunicated from the LDS church, but some Mormon offshoot groups still practice it. Polygamy is permitted in Islam, according to the Quran, which states that men can marry up to four women if they can be “equally just” to all of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give historical and religious context when reporting; be precise about groups and contemporary practices rather than making blanket assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: post-racial
rubrics_metrics.description: A controversial term that describes a society that’s devoid of racial preference, discrimination and prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize controversy; use cautiously and contextualize claims that a society is post-racial.

rubrics_metrics.name: post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
rubrics_metrics.description: An anxiety disorder that can develop after traumatic events such as military combat, natural disasters, terrorist incidents, serious accidents, traumatic brain injury, physical and sexual assault in adults or children, and any other traumatic experience. PTSD can be diagnosed a month or more after the traumatic event has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having PTSD only if relevant to the story and the person has been formally diagnosed by a reputable source. Use 'Post-traumatic stress disorder' on first reference; 'PTSD' thereafter. Use 'flashback' to denote reliving an event that triggered the PTSD when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: poverty line, poverty threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Represents the level of income deemed adequate to live in a particular place. In the U.S. the Federal Poverty Level is calculated every year by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and is used to determine eligibility for federal programs and benefits. Poverty lines are typically anchored to minimum nutritional requirements plus a modest allowance for non-food needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the official term and, when relevant, cite the calculating authority and year; clarify local versus federal thresholds as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: poverty violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fines and fees for petty violations such as fare-hopping on public transit, playing loud music, speeding, driving with a suspended license or expired registration, zoning violations for unkempt property, wearing 'saggy pants,' and failure to appear in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this term to describe how minor infractions and associated penalties can disproportionately affect low-income people; contextualize policy and enforcement patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: powwow
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only when referring to the title of a specific American Indian event. Avoid if referring to a general gathering because the term evokes a stereotypical image of American Indians. Comes from the Narragansett word for shaman. It is a celebration and social gathering, honoring sacred American Indian traditions through dancing, drumming, singing and the gathering of people. A powwow may be held to honor an individual or for a special occasion. Most commonly, it is a social event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict usage to specific event titles; avoid generic use to prevent stereotyping. Provide cultural context and correct capitalization when used as a title.

rubrics_metrics.name: practicing (LGBTQ+)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid this term to describe someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity. Use 'sexually active' as a modifier in circumstances when public awareness of an individual’s behavior is germane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not describe orientation/gender as 'practicing'; reserve 'sexually active' only when behavior (not identity) is newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: pre-lingually deaf/postlingually deaf/late-deafened
rubrics_metrics.description: Prelingually deaf refers to individuals who were born deaf or became deaf prior to learning to understand and speak a language, according to Gallaudet University. Postlingually deaf or late-deafened describes a person who lost hearing ability after he or she learned to speak a language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms are acceptable but may require explanation for general audiences; use accurately and consider people-first language when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: preferred pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the term 'preferred pronouns.' Someone’s pronouns are not a preference, but rather the only appropriate way to refer to that person. The term 'preferred pronouns' is only appropriate when someone uses more than one set of pronouns and has a preference for one over the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'pronouns' instead of 'preferred pronouns.' Updated March 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride Day
rubrics_metrics.description: Short for gay/lesbian pride, this term is commonly used to indicate the celebrations commemorating the Stonewall Inn riots of June 28, 1969. Pride events typically take place in June.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as shorthand for pride celebrations; link to Stonewall and provide date/context where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: primitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using potentially insulting term to describe a person or people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use to describe groups or cultures; choose neutral, specific language.

rubrics_metrics.name: pro-choice
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used to describe people who support abortion rights. Abortion, however, is a more nuanced issue, with many people supporting abortion in some circumstances, but not all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should instead use 'pro-abortion rights' or a similar description, or describe specific views rather than relying on shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: pro-life
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used to describe people who oppose abortion. Abortion, however, is a more nuanced issue, with many people opposing abortion rights in most, but not all, circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a descriptive phrase of views such as 'opposed to abortion' or 'against abortion rights' rather than simplistic labels when precision is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: progressive
rubrics_metrics.description: A term that emerged as a way to refer to people of faith who are liberal-to-moderate in their political views. It is a disputed term because it implies that other groups are regressive, which carries a negative connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use carefully; specify which groups and actions are meant rather than using blanket labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: projects, the
rubrics_metrics.description: This term is commonly used to refer to low-income housing projects. It can carry a negative connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral terms like 'low-income housing project' or 'public housing' instead of 'the projects.'

rubrics_metrics.name: pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: If sources share a transgender or gender-nonconforming identity on the record, ask which pronouns they use and incorporate them into your report as needed. They/them/their are acceptable as nonbinary, singular pronouns if the subject uses them. Alternative nonbinary pronouns, such as zie/zim/zis, are acceptable if requested but may require extra explanation in a story or broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity for the audience. If gender identity is not relevant but a subject uses nonbinary pronouns, consider explaining usage. Avoid 'preferred pronouns' phrasing. Provide suggested recastings and examples; be aware of 'rolling pronouns' and variations. If confused, ask. Updated March 2023.

rubrics_metrics.name: proselytize
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of seeking converts to a faith. Many Christian groups draw a strong distinction between proselytizing and evangelizing. Proselytizing is viewed as the use of unethical methods such as coercion, bribery or threats to bring conversions; evangelizing is considered a pressure-free effort to present the faith and invite others to freely accept it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'proselytize' unless it is being used in a negative context. Prefer 'evangelism' (Protestant) or 'evangelization' (Catholic or Orthodox) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: psycho
rubrics_metrics.description: See crazy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redirects to guidance for 'crazy' — implies colloquial/pejorative term; avoid as insensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: psychotic/psycho
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad term used to describe symptoms of certain mental health problems. Symptoms may include delusions or hallucinations or other loss of contact with reality. People with psychosis are described as psychotic. In common usage, psychotic often is used in the same way as the word crazy, and thus can be offensive and inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'psychotic' and 'psychosis' only when they accurately describe a medical experience. Avoid using 'psychotic' to describe a person; instead say someone 'has a psychotic condition' or 'has psychosis.' Avoid colloquial use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puerto Rico
rubrics_metrics.description: Puerto Rico is a territory of the United States. Spain held Puerto Rico as a colony for more than 400 years and ceded it to the United States in 1898 at the end of the Spanish-American War. It has been under U.S. rule as an unincorporated territory ever since. Puerto Ricans were made citizens in 1917. In 1952, with Congressional approval, Puerto Ricans voted to become a commonwealth. This did not fundamentally change the relationship between Puerto Rico and the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct political status terminology (territory, commonwealth) and historical context when relevant; avoid implying full statehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punjab
rubrics_metrics.description: Both a state in north India and a province in eastern Pakistan. At partition, the British split Punjab, dividing it between the two neighbors. The name Punjab means 'five waters,' or 'five rivers,' and signifies the land drained by the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej rivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about country (India vs. Pakistan) when referring to Punjab; include geographic/historical context as relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punjabi
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary language of Punjab and one of the main regional languages in India. A person from Punjab is referred to as a Punjabi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct demonym and language identifier; distinguish between regional identity and language.

rubrics_metrics.name: qawwali
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'kuh-WAH-lee.' Devotional songs of the Sufi tradition of Islam. Do not capitalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide pronunciation; lowercase the term; give religious/traditional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: quadriplegia/quadriplegic
rubrics_metrics.description: Quadriplegia is defined as the paralysis of all four limbs as well as the torso. It often is caused by a spinal cord or brain injury and is characterized by the loss of sensory and motor function. Paraplegia is similar but does not affect the arms. People with these conditions often are referred to as quadriplegics and paraplegics, but these terms are considered offensive by some.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use people-first language such as 'a person with quadriplegia' rather than labeling someone 'quadriplegic.' If people self-identify with shorthand like 'quads,' use in quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quakers
rubrics_metrics.description: This group’s formal name is the Religious Society of Friends, but Quakers can be used in all references. Members typically refer to themselves as Friends. Historically, Quakers are considered Christian; some Quakers today consider themselves nontheistic. Their worship and business gatherings are called meetings. Although there is no recognized ranking of clergy over lay people, meeting officers are called elders or ministers, and these terms should be capitalized when used before a name. Many Quaker ministers in the Midwest and West use the Rev. before their names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Quakers' or 'Religious Society of Friends' appropriately; capitalize titles before names; be aware of theological diversity within the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: queen
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally a pejorative term for an effeminate gay man but often used acceptably as slang among LGBTQ people. Offensive when used as an epithet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only if there is a compelling reason; avoid as an epithet.

rubrics_metrics.name: queer
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally a pejorative term, queer has been appropriated by some LGBT people as a self-affirming umbrella term. However, it is not universally accepted even within the LGBT community and should be avoided unless describing someone who self-identifies that way or in a direct quote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'queer' only for people who self-identify as such or in quotes; be aware it's not universally accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: quinceañera
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'keen-see-nyair-ah.' A Hispanic celebration of a girl’s 15th birthday, signifying her transition from youth to adulthood. This is both a social and religious event and, like many other Hispanic traditions, emphasizes the importance of family. A quinceañera typically begins with a mass that is attended by the girl’s parents, grandparents, godparents and family. The mass is followed by a reception with food, family, music, dancing and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide pronunciation and cultural/religious context; note historical shifts in meaning and that some families celebrate for boys.

rubrics_metrics.name: quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific or presubscribed number that must be met to reach a certain goal. A buzzword often used in the affirmative action debate, however, it is not synonymous with affirmative action, which is a practice, activity or program aimed at correcting the enduring effects of discrimination and helping to diversify businesses, organizations and schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate 'quotas' from affirmative action; avoid conflating the terms when reporting on diversity policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quran
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'ku-RAHN.' The holy book of Islam, which Muslims believe is the direct word of God as dictated in Arabic to Muhammad by the Angel Gabriel during the month of Ramadan beginning in 610 to about 632. Quran is the preferred spelling and is capitalized in all references. The spelling Koran should only be used if it is in a specific title or name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Quran' (capitalized) and provide pronunciation; avoid older spelling 'Koran' except in titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: rabbi
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebrew word for teacher and the title used by Jewish clergy. On first reference, capitalize before a name. On second reference use only the cleric’s last name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize 'Rabbi' before a name on first reference; use surname on subsequent references.

rubrics_metrics.name: race
rubrics_metrics.description: A person’s race should not be mentioned unless relevant. This also applies to references to ethnicity, sexual orientation and religion. Derogatory terms or slurs aimed at members of a racial or ethnic group may not be used unless having a direct bearing on the news, and then only with the approval of the senior editor in charge. Avoid stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit mention of race/ethnicity/sexual orientation/religion to instances where they are relevant and newsworthy; seek attribution for physical descriptions in crime reporting; avoid overemphasizing race in biographical 'firsts.' See 'ethnicity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: race card, 'play the race card'
rubrics_metrics.description: To say someone is 'playing the race card' is to say they are injecting race into a discussion. To say someone is doing this can be an attempt to deflect, diminish or discredit race’s effects. The expression 'trivializes discussions of racism, implying it’s all just a game.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using the phrase; recognize it can trivialize legitimate discussions of racism and may function as a backlash against talk about race.

rubrics_metrics.name: race, U.S. Census definitions of
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. Census Bureau follows 1997 OMB standards: White; Black or African American; American Indian or Alaska Native; Asian; Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander. The standards permit reporting more than one race and responses are based on self-identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using census categories, adhere to official definitions and note self-identification; list example origins included in each category when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: rainbow flag
rubrics_metrics.description: A flag of six equal horizontal stripes (red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet) symbolizing the diversity of the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as symbol of LGBT community diversity; provide description and color order when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ramadan
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'rah-mah-DAHN.' Islam’s holy month, during which Muslims fast from sunup to sundown. Ramadan commemorates the time during which the faithful believe Allah sent the Angel Gabriel to Muhammad in Mecca and gave him the teachings of the Quran. The end of Ramadan is marked by Eid al-Fitr. Because Islam follows a lunar calendar, Ramadan shifts each year as calculated by Western calendars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide pronunciation, religious significance, fasting practices, and calendar timing; mention Eid al-Fitr as the end-of-month observance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rashomon
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguably the most influential work of fiction on modern journalism. Originally called 'In a Grove' and written by Ryunosuke Akutagawa, the story was made into the acclaimed movie 'Rashomon' (1950). It tells the story of a crime witnessed by different people and their differing memories of the same crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a metaphor for conflicting accounts or differing memories in reporting; provide origin and pronunciation/context if referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rastafarians
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of a political and religious movement among blacks in Jamaica and several other countries. This messianic movement dates back to the 1930s. Rastafarians believe that Haile Selassie is the messiah, consider black people the Israelites reincarnated and have rituals that include the use of marijuana and chanting of revivalist hymns. Reggae music is the popular music of the movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide historical and belief context; avoid stereotyping and be specific about practices and terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Period after the Civil War in which attempts made to rebuild the South and solve the political, social, and economic problems arising from the readmission to the Union of the 11 Confederate states that had seceded. Most historians consider Reconstruction to have taken place 1865-1877.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard historical timeframe and context when referencing Reconstruction; avoid anachronistic or imprecise usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstructionist Judaism
rubrics_metrics.description: A 20th-century movement, founded by Rabbi Mordechai Kaplan, that views Judaism as a social rather than a God-centered phenomenon. Reconstructionists generally do not believe the Hebrew Scriptures are divinely inspired, reject the idea of God as male or female, are less hierarchical and believe that Jewish law as a guiding principle isn’t binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide founder and theological distinctions; identify ordination institution (Reconstructionist Rabbinical College) when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: recovery, treatment (mental illness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recovery from mental illness is a process of change through which individuals improve their health and wellness, live a self-directed life, and strive to reach their full potential. Recognize that a diagnosis of mental illness is not forever. Mental illness is treatable and recovery is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight stories of treatment and recovery to reduce misconceptions; avoid implying permanence or defining people solely by diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: red
rubrics_metrics.description: A good-luck color in several cultures, including Indian and Chinese. It is a favored color for weddings in both cultures and it is the traditional color for the bindi worn by Indian women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cultural color symbolism with context; do not generalize across cultures without specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: redlining
rubrics_metrics.description: Redlining is a discriminatory practice that puts financial services out of reach for residents of certain areas based on race or ethnicity. It can be seen in the systematic denial of mortgages, insurance, loans and other financial services based on location rather than on an individual’s qualifications and creditworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide historical origin and examples; explain mechanisms and racial impact rather than using term vaguely.

rubrics_metrics.name: redneck
rubrics_metrics.description: A derogatory term for whites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use.

rubrics_metrics.name: redskin
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. An overtly racist term that can be compared to the N-word. Some media organizations no longer use the term when referring to the Washington NFL franchise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid term entirely; note Native American Journalists Association guidance and team-name controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redskins (NFL team)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NFL team formerly known as the Washington Redskins announced plans in 2020 to review and then retire the controversial name, temporarily calling itself the 'Washington Football Team' pending adoption of a new name. The team had used the name since 1933 and faced decades of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting, note the name change history and the controversy; avoid using slur name unless necessary for historical context and with editorial approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: rehab
rubrics_metrics.description: See treatment/treatment center/rehab center/detox center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more specific terms such as 'treatment center' rather than colloquial 'rehab' when clarity is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: relationships (LGBTQ+)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lesbian, gay and bisexual people use various terms to describe their commitments. Ask individuals which term they prefer, if possible. If not, 'partner' is generally acceptable. See husband, wife, lover, partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask sources about preferred relationship labels; default to 'partner' when unsure; be precise when sources provide specific terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: religious left
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used to describe people of faith with liberal political views. Journalists can refer to the so-called 'religious left,' but it is best to specify which groups they are referring to and what action they are promoting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about groups and actions rather than relying on vague labels; compare/contrast with 'religious right.'

rubrics_metrics.name: religious right
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used to describe people and groups whose religious beliefs inform their conservative political and social views. Journalists should refer to the so-called 'religious right' or religious conservatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify which groups and actions are meant; avoid vague or stereotypical usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: religious titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on capitalizing and using religious titles across traditions (e.g., Rev., Dr. usage, Buddhist titles, Dalai Lama, Baptist ministers, Islamic titles, Jehovah’s Witnesses, Judaism titles, Nation of Islam, Pentecostalism, Protestant variations, Roman Catholic titles like Pope, cardinals, priests, nuns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize titles before names; do not combine 'Dr.' with other titles; follow tradition-specific practices (e.g., Dalai Lama capitalization, Rev. usage, bishop titles); when in doubt, ask or look up institutional preferences; provide second-reference guidance (usually surname only).

rubrics_metrics.name: reparations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reparations are made to right past wrongs. They are often payments. Examples include payments to black farmers (Pigford v. Glickman), Japanese Americans interned in WWII ($1.6 billion), Native American settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize historical and legal examples; explain scope and precedents when reporting on reparations proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: reservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian reservations are areas of land reserved by the U.S. government as permanent tribal homelands. The United States established its reservation policy for American Indians in 1787. In 2015 there were 326 reservations. About 56 million acres are in reservations and trust land. More than 60 percent of American Indians live away from reservations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct terminology and provide demographic/contextual information; avoid implying all Native Americans live on reservations.

rubrics_metrics.name: residential care homes
rubrics_metrics.description: Residential care homes offer personalized services to small groups of adults who live together in a home. These homes provide lodging, meal services and assistance with daily living activities. Other terms include adult family homes, board and care homes, or personal care homes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific facility types and services when describing care settings; avoid overly broad or misleading labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: retarded
rubrics_metrics.description: See mentally retarded, mentally disabled, intellectually disabled, developmentally disabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference indicates 'retarded' is deprecated/offensive; use people-first and preferred clinical descriptors instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: reverse discrimination, reverse racism
rubrics_metrics.description: These phrases are used in lawsuits and in accusations that affirmative action puts men and non-minorities at a disadvantage for college admission, scholarships and jobs. Research shows that this scarcely happens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using the term, provide data and context; avoid implying symmetry with systemic discrimination without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roma, Romany, Romani
rubrics_metrics.description: The Roma, or Romani (also spelled Romany) are a traditionally itinerant ethnic group, who live mostly in Europe; branches live in the Americas, Asia and North Africa. They are often called Gypsies but that term has negative connotations of illegal activity and many Roma don't identify with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Roma/Romani' rather than 'Gypsies'; provide distinction between Roma and other itinerant groups (e.g., Irish Travelers); include origin and discrimination history when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman Catholic Church
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the largest Christian community in the world and in the U.S. The Roman Catholic Church considers itself to be the one, true, and full expression of the church founded by Jesus Christ. It traces its origins to the Church of Rome and emphasizes papal primacy; Catholic belief and practice are ordered around seven sacraments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide historical and organizational context (Holy See, Vatican, pope, cardinals, archdioceses, dioceses) and canonical practices; use proper capitalization and titles when referencing clergy and offices.
